summary.text: The river of Troy — Xanthos to the gods — whose waters rose against Achilles when corpses choked its banks, until Hephaestus burned the plain to save the son of Peleus.
The Simoeis joins the Scamander before Ilion; its daughters wed into the royal house of Troy — Callirrhoe bore Tros his sons, and Astyoche bore Erichthonius his heir.
The river of Lacedaemon — Eurotas the king who gave his name to the stream that flows past Sparta, where reeds mark the banks of Helen's country.
The river of Elis and Olympia — Alpheus among the great sons of Ocean, whose waters Heracles turned through the cattle-yard of Augeas, and whose god pursued Arethusa to Sicily.
The Thessalian river — father of Daphne, who fled Apollo along its banks and became the laurel at the water's edge; its stream also served Heracles when he cleansed the stables of Augeas.
Chief of the river-gods in Homer — the Achelous of Aetolia and Acarnania, bull-horned suitor of Deianeira, whose broken horn became the Horn of Amalthea.
The winding river of Asia Minor — Maeander among the eddying sons of Ocean in Hesiod's catalogue, its meanders the byword for every turning stream.
The Nile — Nilus in the Greek poets — greatest of the rivers born to Ocean and Tethys, and the flood that feeds Egypt, where Belus wed Anchinoe, daughter of the river, and begat Danaus and Aegyptus.
The river of Argos — son of Ocean in the genealogies, eponym of the oldest royal line, and the witness whose testimony for Hera cost him his springs when Poseidon's anger dried the land.
The Boeotian Asopus — boundary stream between Thebes and Plataea, whose river-god Pausanias names as Antiope's true father, making him grandfather of Amphion and Zethus.
The Attic Cephissus — the Kifisos that watered Athens, one of the three river-judges who awarded Argos to Hera and lost their perennial flow to Poseidon's wrath.
The Malian river beside Thermopylae — where Achilles' mother Thetis dipped the infant in fire and where the river-god Spercheius claimed kinship with the hero.
The great river of Lydia — Hermus in the poets, father of the nymphs who nursed the infant Hermaphroditus and boundary of the kingdom of Croesus.
The river of Ephesus — whose reed-beds Homer knew, and whose banks the Ionian cities claimed as their own.
The throne of Zeus — snow-capped Olympus, highest of the Greek mountains, where the Olympians hold council and mortals dare not climb uninvited.
The double peak above Delphi — seat of Dionysus in winter and refuge of Deucalion's ark when the flood covered the earth.
Many-fountained Ida of Troy — where Paris judged the goddesses, where Anchises kept his flocks, and where Zeus watched the war for Troy from the peaks.
The Boeotian Cephissus — the reed-fringed stream of Orchomenos and the Copaic basin, not to be confused with its Attic namesake.
The Pleistos below Delphi — the river whose valley Apollo chose for his oracle, flowing from the Parnassian heights to the Corinthian Gulf.
The Strymon of Thrace — boundary river in the Argonautica and the march of Xerxes, whose gold-bearing sands and reed beds the poets placed on the northern edge of the Greek world.
Cithaeron — the mountain of Oedipus' exposure and Pentheus' doom, where the Bacchae tore the king apart and the Theban tragedies cast their shadow over Attica and Boeotia.
Taygetus — the long spine of Laconia, where Artemis and the Spartans cast unwanted infants from the peaks and the Pleiad Taygete gave her name to the range.
The Halys of Anatolia — Croesus crossed it to test the oracle and lost his kingdom, and Herodotus made the river the eastern boundary of the Greek-speaking world.
The Thessalian Enipeus — the river beside which Thetis fled from Peleus until Poseidon, who loved the nymph himself, betrayed her hiding place.
The Axios of Macedonia — the Vardar of later ages, whose waters Homer knew as the northern stream beside which the Myrmidons mustered for Troy.
The Sangarius of Phrygia — the great river of the Anatolian interior, beside whose streams Homer sets Hecuba's brother Asius and whose name some authors give as her father.
The Arcadian Ladon — not the serpent of the Hesperides, but the stream near Stymphalus whose naiad Metope married Asopus and whose banks Heracles ran down the Ceryneian Hind.
The Phliasian Asopus — the Sicyonian river whose daughters Aegina, Thebe, and Corcyra the Phliasians count among the Asopids, and whose waters Zeus crossed when he carried Aegina away.

The Orontes of Syria — the Asi of later ages, named among the great rivers of the earth in Hyginus' catalog and burning in Ovid's cosmic fire, while Pausanias knew its Syrian reaches from travellers' reports.
The Ister — the Danube of later ages, listed among the rivers in Hyginus' genealogy, named in Ovid's burning flood, and compared by Pausanias to the great streams of the barbarian north.
The Arcadian Styx — not the whole underworld river but the black waterfall near Nonacris that antiquity identified with the dread stream by which the gods swear their unbreakable oaths.
The Euphrates — the Babylonian stream named among the great rivers in Hyginus' catalog, burning in Ovid's cosmic fire, and measured by Pausanias against the mightiest waters of the barbarian world.
The Tigris — the eastern twin of Mesopotamia, listed with the Euphrates in Hyginus' river genealogy and named among the burning streams of Ovid's heaven-scorching conflagration.
The Jordan — the Hebrew river Pausanias saw pass through the lake of Tiberias and vanish into the Dead Sea on his travels in the eastern lands.
The Araxes — the loud-roaring stream of the Caucasus whose outfall Apollonius places beside Colchis, where the Lycus parts from it and blends his waters with the Phasis.

The Eridanus of Phaethon's fall — the river into which the son of Helios plunged when Zeus struck him from the chariot; Hyginus names the Padus of Italy as the Greek Eridanus, and Ovid and Apollodorus tell the burning of the sky above its banks.
Pelion — the forested mountain where the Centaurs dwelt, where Peleus won Thetis, and where the Argonauts' ship Argo was built from its timber.
Helicon — the Boeotian mountain of the Muses, where Hesiod was given the staff of laurel and where the Pierian springs first flowed.
Oeta — the Malian mountain where Heracles ascended his own pyre and was taken up to Olympus, and where Pausanias traced the hero's last path through Trachis.
The Pindus — the great spine of mainland Greece dividing Epirus from Thessaly, named among the mountains scorched in Ovid's heaven-fire.
Athos — the holy peak of the Chalcidice peninsula whose shadow Homer knew when Hera swore her oath upon Styx, and where the Argonauts held course along the coast.
Etna of Sicily — the burning mountain under which Apollodorus buries Typhon and from whose forge the gods' thunderbolts were wrought, a beacon of fire visible across the strait.
The Atlas range of Libya — the western mountains that bear the Titan's name, where Hesiod set Atlas holding up heaven and Homer placed the orchard of his daughter near the world's edge.
The Caucasus — the eastern mountains where Apollodorus bound Prometheus to the rock and the Argonauts heard the clash of bronze wings on their voyage toward Colchis.
Parnes — the Attic mountain north of Athens where Pausanias traced cults and fortifications guarding the passes into Boeotia.

The Thesprotian Acheron — into which Periphlegethon and Cocytus flow in Homer's house of Hades, and beside whose lake Acherusia Pausanias placed the sights that he believed the poet had seen before he described the underworld.
Cocytus — the most unlovely stream of Thesprotia, a branch of the water of Styx in Homer's necromancy, which Pausanias saw near Cichyrus beside the Acheron and the lake Acherusia.
